title: The god who thought he was permanent
hook: Baka the Brahma believes his heaven eternal; the Buddha shows him otherwise

segments.voice: Yesterday: verbal daggers, and the six qualities that put them down. Your line: verbal daggers down. Today ends a week, with a god who was very sure of himself.

Somewhere there's a person who has lived in the same town all their life and will tell you, kindly and firmly, that it's the best place in the world. They may be right. But they've never been anywhere else, so how would they know? Now make that person a god, living in a radiant heaven so long that he's forgotten arriving. His name is Baka, a Brahma god, and he has a theory about his home.
screen: `THE BEST PLACE IN THE WORLD.` → `BUT NEVER BEEN ANYWHERE ELSE.` → `BAKA, A BRAHMA GOD, AND HIS THEORY.`

segments.voice: This is the forty-ninth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the invitation of a Brahma. Baka holds this view: this place is permanent, eternal, complete. Here nobody is born, ages or dies, and there's no escape beyond it, because nothing is beyond it. The Buddha, knowing the god's thought, appears in his heaven. Baka welcomes him warmly and repeats his claim. Baka has fallen into ignorance, the Buddha says: he calls permanent what is impermanent. Then Mara, the tempter, slips into the scene, speaking through one of the god's assembly: don't contradict the Brahma, he's the creator, the lord of all. The Buddha sees through it. I know you, Mara. Then he shows Baka what Baka hasn't seen. There are other realms, higher and more radiant, which you don't know and can't see. And you yourself once lived in one of them, and have forgotten. Then comes a contest. Baka says: I'll vanish from you. He can't. The Buddha says: I'll vanish from you. He does, and speaks a verse, his voice heard while his body can't be seen. The god and his whole assembly are astonished. Under the drama is the point. Even a long, bright life in a heaven is still a life: arisen, and so it will pass. Baka wasn't wicked. He was comfortable, and comfort mistook itself for forever. Look back at this week: a true samana, ten courses, Dhammadinna, four drinks, a teacher examined, daggers set down. Each pointed past something that only looked final.
screen: `BAKA: THIS PLACE IS ETERNAL` · `MARA SPEAKS THROUGH THE ASSEMBLY` · `REALMS YOU DON'T KNOW, LIVES YOU FORGOT` · `THE GOD CAN'T VANISH; THE BUDDHA CAN` · then, large: `NOTHING IS FOREVER.`

segments.voice: Find one thing it's easy to assume will always be there, your health, a parent, your job, this exact version of yourself, name it quietly, and add: for now. My health, for now. This friendship, for now. Don't panic or argue; notice whether it feels sadder, or more precious, or both, and let it rest with the breath.
Anicca. Impermanent: what Baka the Brahma, so long in his bright heaven, mistook for eternal.
Your line: nothing is forever. Even a god's long, bright life arises and passes. That's a week.

howItsDone: In Buddhist cosmology even the Brahma gods live long but finite lives; teachers use stories like Baka's to show that no state of existence, however blissful, is permanent, and reflection on impermanence (anicca) is a traditional meditation subject.

original.note: Pali anicca: impermanent. Baka calls permanent what the Buddha calls anicca.

what a scholar hears: MN 49 shows a Brahma god holding an eternalist view, and the story of Baka also appears in the Samyutta Nikaya (SN 6.4), where the Buddha recalls Baka's past good deeds.

chat.says: Do Buddhists believe the gods live forever?
options: In the stories, gods live long, bright lives, but even they arise and pass.
Yes; Baka's heaven is eternal, and the Buddha agreed with him.
No; Buddhists say the gods are wicked and should be ignored.
chat.meaning: In MN 49 the Buddha tells Baka he calls permanent what is impermanent; even a long life in a heaven has arisen, and will pass.

Baka.meaning: a Brahma god who thought his heaven was eternal

Brahma.meaning: a high god of the old Indian heavens

samana.meaning: a wanderer who left home to seek truth

Dhammadinna.meaning: a nun who answered deep questions about the teaching
